title: Shortest Directed Paths: Scale and Continuum Limits
result_html:
Let \(M\) be the uniform infinite bipolar-oriented triangulation. Let \(\Delta_n\) be the maximum finite vertex-to-vertex shortest directed-path distance in the unconditioned KMSW cell encoded by \(n\) independent increments, each uniform on \(\{(1,-1),(-1,0),(0,1)\}\). The cell contains its \(n+1\) active edges with their endpoint identifications; missing boundary edges are excluded.

The distance scale. There are deterministic constants \(c,C>0\) such that, for every \(n\ge0\) and \(A\ge1\), \[\mathbb P\!\left[\Delta_n>A(n+1)^{3/8}\right]\le C e^{-cA}.\] For every deterministic choice of medians \(m_n\) of \(\Delta_n\), \[c n^{3/8}\le m_n\le C n^{3/8},\qquad n\ge1.\] The constants do not depend on the chosen medians.

Continuous subsequential limits. Write \(p(e)=(i(e),j(e))\) for the north- and west-going primal Peano times of an edge, rooted at the same edge and oriented to increase along directed paths. Let \(d_M^\bullet(e,f)\) count the minimum number of edges in a directed path starting with \(e\) and ending with \(f\), with \(d_M^\bullet(e,e)=1\). Set \[\begin{aligned} U_n&=\{p(e)/n:e\in E(M)\},\\ W_n&=\{(x,y)\in U_n^2:x\le y\},\\ D_n\!\left(\frac{p(e)}n,\frac{p(f)}n\right)&=\frac{d_M^\bullet(e,f)}{m_n}. \end{aligned}\] Here \(x\le y\) is coordinatewise, and \(\Gamma_n=\operatorname{Graph}(W_n,D_n)\).

The laws of \((W_n,\Gamma_n)\) are tight in \(\mathcal F(\mathbb R^4)\times\mathcal F(\mathbb R^5)\), where \(\mathcal F\) denotes closed subsets with the Fell topology. Every subsequential weak limit is almost surely \[(W,\operatorname{Graph}(W,D)),\] where \(D:W\to[0,\infty)\) is locally bounded and continuous. Every point of the limiting domain has exactly one finite limiting height.

Nontriviality. Every such limiting function is almost surely not identically zero: \[\mathbb P\!\left[\exists\,x\ne y:\ (x,y)\in W,\ D(x,y)>0\right]=1.\] Section 8 derives this from the preceding scale, locality, transverse-compactness, and graph-limit results using independent marked cells. No additional joint convergence with quantum-surface data is assumed.

The limiting graph determines a unique function. Uniqueness of the subsequential law and positive distance for every distinct comparable pair are not asserted.

title: The Small-γ LQG Dimension Expansion
description:
Proposed asymptotic.  Let \(d_\gamma\) denote the almost sure Hausdorff dimension of the planar \(\gamma\)-Liouville quantum gravity metric, with the Gaussian free field normalized to have logarithmic covariance singularity \(\log(1/|z-w|)\). As \(\gamma\downarrow 0\), the proposed expansion is
\[ d_\gamma=2+k\gamma^{4/3}+o(\gamma^{4/3}), \]
where \(k\) is a deterministic, strictly positive, finite constant. 
 The coefficient is characterized by a Gaussian variational problem. Let \(V_n\) consist of continuous functions on \([0,1]\) that vanish at the endpoints and are affine on each interval of the uniform mesh \(16^{-n}\). Let \((Z_f)\) be the centered Gaussian family with covariance
\[ \begin{aligned}\operatorname{Cov}(Z_f,Z_g)\\ &=\pi\int_0^1\bigl(|f|+|g|-|f-g|\bigr)\,dx.\end{aligned} \]
and set
\[ a_n=\mathbb{E}\sup_{f\in V_n}\left\{Z_f-\frac12\int_0^1|f'|^2\,dx\right\}. \]
The stated theorem gives
\[ \begin{aligned}
0<a_*&=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{a_n}{n}=\inf_{n\geq1}\frac{a_n}{n}<\infty,\\
k&=\frac{2^{-1/3}a_*}{\log16}.
\end{aligned} \] 
 Equivalently, the planar LFPP exponent satisfies
\[ \frac{\lambda(\xi)}{\xi^{4/3}}\longrightarrow\frac{a_*}{\log16}\quad\text{as }\xi\downarrow0, \]
with parameter relation
\[ \begin{aligned}
\xi&=\frac{\gamma}{d_\gamma},\\
\lambda(\gamma/d_\gamma)&=1-\frac{2+\gamma^2/2}{d_\gamma}.
\end{aligned} \]
This specifies a leading coefficient; its numerical value is not evaluated in the note.

title: Gaussian Fluctuations of LQG Distance
description:
Proposed theorem.  Let \(h\) be a whole-plane Gaussian free field with unit-circle average \(h_1(0)=0\). For each \(0<\gamma<2\), let \(D_h^\gamma\) be the \(\gamma\)-LQG metric, using the same field for all \(\gamma\). Fix its deterministic scale by requiring the lower median of
\[ C_\gamma=\inf_{s,t\in[0,1]}D_h^\gamma(is,1+it) \]
to equal one. These are global distances: the connecting paths are not required to stay inside the unit square. 
 Define
\[ H_y=\int_0^1 h(x+iy)\,dx \]
by \(L^2\) limits of smooth mollifications, and let \(q\) be the lower median of \(\min_{y\in[0,1]}H_y\). The proposed result states that \(q<0\) and
\[ \frac{D_h^\gamma(0,1)-1}{\gamma}\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}\frac{H_0-q}{2} \]
as \(\gamma\downarrow0\) on the common field probability space. 
 Consequently the limiting distribution is Gaussian with mean \(-q/2\) and variance \(3/8\). The point-distance median \(m_\gamma=\operatorname{med}D_h^\gamma(0,1)\) also satisfies
\[ m_\gamma=1-\frac{q}{2}\gamma+o(\gamma). \]
Thus the first-order normalization correction comes from minimizing horizontal line integrals across the square.

title: Two-Thirds Geodesic Deviation
description:
Let \(h\) be a whole-plane Gaussian free field with \(h_1(0)=0\), and let \(P_\gamma\) be its \(\gamma\)-LQG geodesic from \(0\) to \(1\), regarded as an unparametrized curve. Set
\[ M_\gamma=\max_{z\in P_\gamma}\operatorname{dist}(z,[0,1]), \]
the largest Euclidean distance from the straight segment. This quantity is unchanged by multiplying the metric by a positive factor. 
 There are deterministic \(C<\infty\) and \(\gamma_0>0\) such that
\[ \mathbb{E}M_\gamma\leq C\gamma^{2/3},\qquad 0<\gamma<\gamma_0, \]
and
\[ \mathbb{P}\!\left[M_\gamma\leq a\gamma^{2/3}\right]\leq Ca^{3/5} \]
uniformly over \(0<a\leq1\) and \(0<\gamma<\gamma_0\). For every \(A\geq1\), the sharper upper-tail statement is
\[ \begin{aligned}\limsup_{\gamma\downarrow0}\mathbb{P}\!\left[M_\gamma>A\gamma^{2/3}\right]\\ &\leq C(A^{-3}+A^{-4}).\end{aligned} \] 
 Consequently \(M_\gamma/\gamma^{2/3}\) is tight and uniformly bounded away from zero in probability as \(\gamma\downarrow0\). Every subsequential weak limit is finite and strictly positive almost surely, and the inverse moments of orders \(0<r<3/5\) are uniformly bounded for \(0<\gamma<\gamma_0\). The theorem does not assert convergence to a unique law or exclude a positive deterministic subsequential limit.

title: Tightness of Small-Parameter Geodesics
description:
Let \(h\) be a whole-plane Gaussian free field with \(h_1(0)=0\), and let \(P_\gamma\) be the almost surely unique \(\gamma\)-LQG geodesic from \(0\) to \(1\). Parametrize it on \([0,1]\) at constant metric speed, so
\[ D_h^\gamma\bigl(0,P_\gamma(t)\bigr)=tD_h^\gamma(0,1). \]
Multiplying the metric by a positive constant does not change this parametrized path. 
 The family
\[ X_\gamma(t)=\gamma^{-2/3}\bigl(P_\gamma(t)-t\bigr) \]
is tight in \(C([0,1],\mathbb{R}^2)\), with its uniform topology, as \(\gamma\downarrow0\). Moreover,
\[ \sup_{t\in[0,1]}\frac{|\operatorname{Re}P_\gamma(t)-t|}{\gamma^{2/3}}\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}0, \]
so any subsequential limit has zero horizontal component. The functional statement includes control of the modulus of continuity and uses the constant-speed parametrization; it does not identify a unique limiting law. 
 The proof imports the scalar mean bound, clock geometry, and frequency-localized estimate from the two-thirds-deviation note. Its additional conclusion is tightness of the entire rescaled path, beyond tightness of its maximum deviation.

title: Conformal Covariance of Supercritical LQG
description:
Fix \(\xi>\xi_{\mathrm{crit}}\) with \(Q=Q(\xi)\in(0,2)\), and use one fixed normalization of the canonical supercritical Liouville quantum gravity metric. Let \(U,V\subset\mathbb{C}\) be domains, let \(\varphi:U\to V\) be a fixed deterministic conformal bijection, and let \(h\) be a Gaussian free field plus a continuous function on \(V\), in the local sense required to define the metric. Here \(D_h(x,y;V)\) is the internal distance, obtained by minimizing metric length over paths contained in \(V\); it may equal \(+\infty\). 
 Almost surely, simultaneously for every \(u,v\in U\),
\[ \begin{aligned}
D_h\bigl(\varphi(u),\varphi(v);V\bigr)\\
&\quad=D_{h\circ\varphi+Q\log|\varphi'|}(u,v;U).
\end{aligned} \]
The multiplicative constant is exactly one, and the equality includes singular endpoints and infinite distances. The probability-one event may depend on \(\varphi\); the statement is for each fixed map.

title: Higher-Dimensional LFPP Exponents
description:
Fix a dimension \(d\geq2\) and normalize the whole-space log-correlated Gaussian field to have covariance singularity \(\log(1/|x-y|)\). Let \(H_N\) be its smooth white-noise cutoff from scales \(2^{-N}\) to \(1\), using a fixed smooth compactly supported radial kernel as specified in the note, so \(\operatorname{Var}H_N(x)=N\log2\). Let \(a_N(\xi)\) be the median of
\[ \inf_{\substack{P:0\to e_1\\P\subset(-2,2)^d}}\int_P e^{\xi H_N(z)}\,|dz|, \]
where \(e_1\) is the first coordinate unit vector and the infimum is over rectifiable paths. Define
\[ \begin{aligned}
\lambda_d(\xi)&=-\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{\log a_N(\xi)}{N\log2}\\
&=1-\xi Q_d(\xi).
\end{aligned} \] 
 For each fixed \(d\) there are constants \(c_d,C_d>0\) and \(\xi_d>0\) such that
\[ \frac{c_d\xi^{4/3}}{\log(1/\xi)}\leq\lambda_d(\xi)\leq C_d\xi^{4/3} \]
whenever \(0<\xi<\xi_d\). In particular, \(\log\lambda_d(\xi)/\log\xi\to4/3\). The constants and the small-parameter threshold may depend on \(d\). 
 Under the metric-dimension correspondence
\[ Q_d(\xi)=\frac{d}{\gamma}+\frac{\gamma}{2},\qquad \xi=\frac{\gamma}{d_\gamma}, \]
the same type of bounds holds for \(d_\gamma-d\):
\[ \frac{c'_d\gamma^{4/3}}{\log(1/\gamma)}\leq d_\gamma-d\leq C'_d\gamma^{4/3} \]
for sufficiently small \(\gamma\). These are logarithmic-exponent conclusions; the note does not identify a leading coefficient or establish convergence of \(\lambda_d(\xi)/\xi^{4/3}\).

title: An Axiomatic Metric in Higher Dimensions
description:
Proposed theorem.  Fix \(d\geq 3\) and \(\xi>0\) such that the continuum LFPP distance exponent satisfies \(Q=Q(\xi)>\sqrt{2d}\). The underlying field is the whole-space log-correlated Gaussian field on \(\mathbb{R}^d\), with covariance kernel \(\log(1/|x-y|)\) modulo constants. The proposed result constructs a measurable assignment \(h\mapsto D_h\) of finite metrics inducing the Euclidean topology, defined for this field plus continuous functions. 
 The assignment satisfies four strong axioms: \(D_h\) is a length metric; its internal metric in each deterministic open set \(U\) is determined by \(h\) restricted to \(U\); adding a continuous \(f\) reweights path length by \(e^{\xi f}\); and, for each fixed \(r>0\) and \(z\in\mathbb{R}^d\),
\[ \begin{aligned} D_h(ru+z,rv+z)\\ &\quad=D_{h(r\cdot+z)+Q\log r}(u,v). \end{aligned} \]
almost surely for all \(u,v\). 
 Any two assignments satisfying these axioms at the same parameters are proposed to differ by a deterministic positive factor, simultaneously for all endpoint pairs and continuous field perturbations. For the continuum approximation kernels specified in the manuscript, the proposed result also gives convergence in probability of normalized LFPP metrics, locally uniformly, to this assignment. The approximation assertion is restricted to those kernels.

title: Sphere Averages in Odd Dimensions
description:
Let \(h\) be the whole-space log-correlated Gaussian field on \(\mathbb{R}^d\), with covariance kernel \(\log(1/|x-y|)\) modulo an additive constant, and let \(h_r(0)\) denote its spherical average. For odd \(d=2m+1\geq 3\), set \(S_t=h_{e^{-t}}(0)-h_1(0)\), \(t\in\mathbb{R}\). As a continuous process, \(S\) has the same law as
\[ \int_0^\infty q_d(u)\bigl(B_{t-u}-B_{-u}\bigr)\,du, \]
where \(B\) is standard two-sided Brownian motion and
\[ q_d(u)=(d-2)e^{-2u}(1-e^{-2u})^{(d-4)/2},\quad u>0. \] 
 The process has a modification locally in \(C^{m-1,\alpha}\) for every \(0<\alpha<1\). The increment variance of its \((m-1)\)st derivative is comparable to \(r^2\log(1/|r|)\) as \(r\to 0\), uniformly in the base time. An \(m\)th derivative does not exist in the mean-square sense. 
 The note also computes the exact spectrum of the generalized derivative of \(S\). In odd dimensions this spectrum is nonrational, excluding a finite-dimensional linear Gaussian state-space realization; an explicit time-homogeneous Markov representation is instead constructed using an infinite-dimensional memory profile.

title: Quantum Cones in Odd Dimensions
description:
Let \(d\geq 3\) be odd, let \(0<\gamma<\sqrt{2d}\), and fix \(\beta<Q=d/\gamma+\gamma/2\). For a whole-space log-correlated Gaussian field \(h\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\), normalized by \(h_1(0)=0\), write \(S_t=h_{e^{-t}}(0)\). For \(b>0\), define
\[ \begin{aligned}
\sigma_b&=\inf\{t\in\mathbb{R}:S_t-(Q-\beta)t=-b\},\\
S_{b,s}&=S_{s+\sigma_b}-S_{\sigma_b}.
\end{aligned} \] 
 For each fixed \(T\in\mathbb{R}\), the law of \((S_{b,s})_{s\geq T}\) converges in total variation as \(b\to\infty\). These limits are compatible as \(T\) varies and define a continuous process \(S_\infty\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) with \(S_{\infty,0}=0\). The \(\beta\)-quantum cone is obtained by taking spherical averages \(S_{\infty,s}+\beta s\) and adding an independent copy of the field’s projection with zero average on every centered sphere. 
 More precisely, set
\[ \begin{aligned}
h^{(b)}(x)&=h(e^{-\sigma_b}x)-\beta\log|e^{-\sigma_b}x|\\
&\qquad-Q\sigma_b+b.
\end{aligned} \]
On every fixed ball \(B(0,R)\), the law of \(h^{(b)}\), viewed as a random distribution, converges in total variation to the cone field normalized to have unit-sphere average zero. The same local-limit statement holds about any fixed deterministic center after translating and normalizing the original field there.

title: Mesh-Only Convergence for Orthogonal Tilings
description:
Let \(d\ge2\) and let \(D\subset\mathbb R^d\) be open. Consider locally finite orthogonal tilings of \(D\) by closed convex polytopes \(P_v\) with marked points \(v\) in their interiors: cells are joined across shared facets, and the line between their marked points is perpendicular to the shared facet. Give each edge the conductance \[a(v,w)=\frac{\operatorname{vol}_{d-1}(P_v\cap P_w)}{|v-w|}.\] Assume only that the maximum tile diameter \(\varepsilon_n\) tends to zero, with no additional cell-shape or cell-volume alternative. 
 Fix a bounded open \(U\) with closure compactly contained in \(D\), and a fixed bounded open neighborhood \(K\) of the closure of \(U\) with closure compactly contained in \(D\). Let \(h\) be harmonic and \(C^2\) on a neighborhood of the closure of \(K\). For sufficiently large \(n\), there is a unique discrete harmonic function \(h_n\) on the vertices in \(U\), with boundary values \(h\) at adjacent vertices outside \(U\). The full note proves uniform convergence to \(h\). The recovered supplement sharpens its quantitative bound to \[\begin{aligned}&\max_{v\in V_n\cap U}|h_n(v)-h(v)|\\&\qquad\le C_{d,U,K}\,\lVert h\rVert_{C^2(K)}\,\varepsilon_n^{4/(d+4)}.\end{aligned}\] Thus the planar exponent is \(2/3\). The 17-page note itself prints the earlier exponent \(4/(3d+8)\); the three-page supplement supplies the sharper argument using estimates proved in that note. 
 The mesh-only approximation also verifies the harmonic-approximation input used for uniform convergence of harmonic measure on balls and convergence of the stopped canonical walk, whose transition probabilities are proportional to \(a(v,w)\). These consequences retain the remaining domain hypotheses of the cited Bou-Rabee–Gwynne results; walk convergence is to Brownian motion modulo time parametrization. The exponent \(2/3\) bounds the harmonic-extension error and is not a rate of convergence for a parametrized random walk. The full note and supplement are complementary: the supplement does not replace the analytic estimates or the walk-convergence argument.

title: Sphere Packings and Tangency-Polytope Tilings
description:
Let \(d\in\{2,3,4\}\), let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\) be any nonempty open set, and fix \(\varepsilon>0\). There is a countably infinite family of closed balls \(B(v,r_v)\subset\Omega\) with pairwise disjoint interiors and \(0\lt r_v\le\varepsilon\). For each ball, intersect the halfspaces bounded by its common tangent hyperplanes with all tangent balls, choosing the halfspace containing \(B(v,r_v)\). The resulting tangency polytope \(P_v\) is bounded, and the polytopes form a locally finite, face-to-face tiling of exactly \(\Omega\). 
 Two balls are tangent if and only if their polytopes share a facet, and that facet lies in their common tangent hyperplane. Consequently, joining the ball centers across shared facets gives an orthogonal tiling graph. In dimensions 2, 3, and 4 respectively, each tile has at most 6, 12, and 24 facets, and \[B(v,r_v)\subset P_v\subset B(v,C_d r_v),\] where \(C_2=2\), \(C_3=\sqrt{10}\), and \(C_4=3\sqrt2+2\). 
 No boundedness, connectedness, or boundary-regularity assumption on \(\Omega\) is required. Local finiteness is relative to \(\Omega\), so accumulation at its boundary is allowed. Exact coverage is by the tangency polytopes; the balls need not cover \(\Omega\). The three PDFs give separate constructions in the three dimensions. The four-dimensional construction includes an exact-integer computer-assisted interpolation step and its complete checker.

In dimensions 2, 3, and 4 respectively, each tile has at most 6, 12, and 24 facets, and \[B(v,r_v)\subset P_v\subset B(v,C_d r_v),\] where \(C_2=2\), \(C_3=\sqrt{10}\), and \(C_4=3\sqrt2+2\).

No boundedness, connectedness, or boundary-regularity assumption on \(\Omega\) is required. Local finiteness is relative to \(\Omega\), so accumulation at its boundary is allowed. Exact coverage is by the tangency polytopes; the balls need not cover \(\Omega\). The three PDFs give separate constructions in the three dimensions. The four-dimensional construction includes an exact-integer computer-assisted interpolation step and its complete checker.

title: Reflected Random Walks with Spatial Singularities
description:
Consider a random countable collection of compact connected planar cells with nonempty interiors, disjoint interiors, and boundaries of zero area. Adjacent cells are distinct and intersect, their adjacency graph is connected and locally finite, and each adjacent pair \(H,K\) has a symmetric conductance \(c(H,K)>0\). The  singular-set version  assumes a closed set \(S\) with one-dimensional Hausdorff measure \(\mathcal H^1(S)=0\), coverage of \(\mathbb C\setminus S\), spatial local finiteness off \(S\), and connectedness of the induced cell graph along every horizontal or vertical segment avoiding \(S\). The  whole-plane version  instead requires coverage of all \(\mathbb C\) and connectedness along every segment on almost every horizontal and vertical line; it allows spatial accumulation without a closed \(\mathcal H^1\)-null witness. These are distinct geometric hypotheses. 
 In either version, assume mass transport modulo translations and positive dilations and ergodicity under these similarities. Write \(a_H=\operatorname{Area}(H)\), \(\pi(H)=\sum_{K\sim H}c(H,K)\), and \(\pi^*(H)=\sum_{K\sim H}c(H,K)^{-1}\). If \(H_0\) is the almost surely unique cell whose interior contains the origin, the required moment is \[\mathbb E\!\left[\frac{\operatorname{diam}(H_0)^2}{a_{H_0}}\bigl(\pi(H_0)+\pi^*(H_0)\bigr)\right]\lt\infty.\] The singular-set paper also specifies its geometric environment topology and a measurable full-probability class admitting the required witnesses; it derives graph local finiteness and the null-boundary property from its hypotheses. 
 Conditionally on almost every environment, the canonical walk reflected off infinity has a conservative area clock, with transition rate \(c(H,K)/a_H\) and mean holding time \(a_H/\pi(H)\). Choose representatives inside the cells, interpolate ordinary jumps, and extend the spatial path through reflection times as in the construction. From every fixed starting cell, \(\bigl(\varepsilon Z_{t/\varepsilon^2}\bigr)_{t\ge0}\) converges in law, locally uniformly in time as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), to Brownian motion with a deterministic finite positive-definite covariance matrix \(\Sigma\). Assigning the exact holding time \(a_H/\pi(H)\) at every visit gives the same limit and the same \(\Sigma\). Neither manuscript asserts uniformity over starting cells chosen as a function of \(\varepsilon\).
